questions.title: Why could the TTAB treat "credit card services" and "banking and financing services" as legally identical in part?
questions.question_body: I'm confused about the court's affirmance on the second DuPont factor. CC Serve does not seem to operate as a traditional bank, and the opinion says it partners with a bank that actually issues the ASPIRE-branded cards. Apex, by contrast, applied for "banking and financing services" and apparently does not even offer credit cards right now. So how did the Board and the Federal Circuit get to the conclusion that the services are "legally identical, in part"? Is this because trademark law looks only at the wording in the application/registration rather than the parties' real-world business models, or was there something else going on?

questions.title: In a Section 2(d) opposition, how much do the applicant's actual planned services matter compared with the identification of services in the application?
questions.question_body: Apex argued that the parties' services were not directly competitive and that CC Serve was really managing card programs rather than providing banking services itself. But the court seemed to focus heavily on the listed services and dictionary definitions instead. In TTAB opposition proceedings, is the tribunal generally required to compare the application and registration as written, even if the evidence shows the parties' actual businesses are narrower? If so, are there any limits on that rule?

questions.title: Why was the Board's sixth DuPont factor analysis a legal error rather than just a factual judgment about weak evidence?
questions.question_body: The Federal Circuit said the Board committed legal error by limiting the sixth factor to third-party Aspire marks used only for credit card services, instead of also considering banking and financing services that the Board had already found highly similar. I don't fully understand why this is classified as a legal flaw instead of just a debatable factual weighing of relevance. Was the problem that the Board applied the wrong legal standard for what counts as "similar goods or services" under factor six?

questions.title: Does the sixth DuPont factor require evidence of use in the exact same market, or just use on sufficiently similar goods/services?
questions.question_body: The opinion says the sixth factor concerns the "number and nature of similar marks in use on similar goods," and it cites cases saying the goods do not need to be identical. I'm trying to pin down the rule. If a party is trying to show that a cited mark is commercially weak because the field is crowded, how close do the third-party uses have to be? Would use on general financial services, fintech, lending, or banking all potentially count against strength of ASPIRE here, even if they are not literally credit card services?

questions.title: Why did the Federal Circuit also vacate the first DuPont factor without deciding for itself whether the marks ASPIRE and ASPIRE BANK are similar?
questions.question_body: On the marks themselves, I would have thought the court could separately analyze whether ASPIRE and ASPIRE BANK are similar in sight, sound, connotation, and commercial impression. Instead, it said the first-factor analysis had to be vacated because reconsideration of factor six could change the mark's commercial strength or weakness and therefore the commercial impression analysis. How exactly does evidence of third-party Aspire marks feed into the first-factor comparison of the two marks themselves?

questions.title: What is the practical difference between a mark's 'commercial strength,' 'conceptual strength,' and the 'normal scope of protection' the Board mentioned?
questions.question_body: The Board said CC Serve had not shown any particular commercial strength, but Apex had also not shown that ASPIRE was commercially or conceptually weak, so the mark got the normal scope of protection for an inherently distinctive mark. I'm having trouble separating these concepts. What does it mean for a mark to be conceptually weak versus commercially weak, and how does that affect the breadth of protection in a likelihood-of-confusion analysis?

questions.title: Why didn't the Federal Circuit simply reverse the likelihood-of-confusion finding if the Board mishandled two important DuPont factors?
questions.question_body: The court affirmed factor two, vacated factors six and one, and remanded, rather than holding outright that confusion either was or was not likely. Since likelihood of confusion is ultimately a legal question, why couldn't the Federal Circuit resolve it on appeal once it found errors in the Board's analysis? Is this because the underlying DuPont findings are fact-intensive and the appellate court wanted the Board to evaluate the third-party evidence first?
